title: PRICE TRACKER (CAMELCAMELCAMEL)
subtitle: Five hundred million products can't all be crawled often, so decide what is worth checking.
footer: DDIA: Ch 11 event-driven · Ch 3 time-series storage   ·   Similar: Top-K videos · Ad click aggregator · Web crawler · Metrics monitoring

items: Prioritise crawling by how many people track a product and how often its price changes.
Add crowd-sourced prices from a browser extension, validated before they trigger alerts.
Make alerts event-driven: when a price drops, look up subscriptions for that product only.
Track price history for products
Users subscribe to alerts at a target price
View price charts
500M products
Alert within ~1 hour of a drop
Respect site rate limits (crawl budget)
Charts load fast
500M products crawled daily = ~6k pages/s, which runs into rate limits.
Subscriptions are concentrated on a small fraction of products, so prioritize those.

POST /subscriptions {product_id, target_price}

price_history(product_id, ts, price) time-series
subscriptions(product_id, user_id, target_price) indexed (product_id, target_price)
A scheduler decides what to crawl: products with many subscribers or volatile prices are checked more often; the long tail rarely.
A browser extension reports prices users actually see, which adds coverage for free. Validate it (N agreeing reports or a crawler re-check) before trusting it.

items: A browser extension reports prices users actually see, which adds coverage for free.
Every price change becomes an event; history goes to a time-series table (downsampled for charts).
Alerts are event-driven: on a drop, query subscriptions WHERE product_id=? AND target_price ≥ new_price and notify, deduped per user and product.
Crawl budget?
Prioritize by subscribers and volatility; adaptive frequency; respect robots and rate limits.
Bad extension data?
Require agreement or confirm with a crawl before alerting.
Matching efficiently?
Index on (product_id, target_price); react to events, never scan all subscriptions.
Charts?
Daily aggregates, cached.
Re-scanning all subscriptions on a schedule instead of reacting to price changes.
Adding parts before a number shows they are needed.
Ignoring retries, timeouts and crashes.
